This marriage is the right thing. I disagreed at first, but now I admit it. The gods created Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, something would always have been missing from your life.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, squeezing his hand. “I knew you would understand. Harry’s cynicism frightens me. But the orchestra is starting. It’s dreadful, though it only goes on for about five minutes. Then the curtain will go up, and you’ll see the girl I’m going to devote my whole life to, the girl I’ve already given everything good in me.”

Fifteen minutes later, Sibyl Vane walked onto the stage to a tremendous burst of applause. She certainly was beautiful—one of the most beautiful people Lord Henry had ever seen, he thought. Her shy grace and wide, startled eyes reminded him of a young deer. As she looked out at the eager, crowded theatre, a delicate blush spread over her cheeks, like a rose faintly reflected in silver. She retreated a few steps, and her lips seemed to shake. Basil Hallward sprang up and clapped. Dorian Gray remained completely still, staring at her as though dreaming. Lord Henry looked through his glasses and whispered, “Charming! Charming!”

The setting was the hall in Capulet’s house. Romeo had arrived dressed as a pilgrim, accompanied by Mercutio and his other friends. The band, poor as it was, played a few opening notes, and the dancing started. Among the awkward actors in their shabby costumes, Sibyl Vane seemed to belong to a more beautiful world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant beneath the water. Her neck curved like a white lily, and her hands looked as though they were carved from cool ivory.

Yet there was a strange lack of energy in her. When she looked at Romeo, she showed no happiness. The few lines she had to speak—

“Good pilgrim, you judge your hand too harshly; its touch shows courteous devotion. Saints have hands that pilgrims touch, and when their palms meet, that is the holy pilgrim’s kiss”—

and the short exchange that followed sounded completely unnatural. Her voice itself was lovely, but the way she used it was entirely false. Its emotional colouring was wrong. It drained the poetry of life and made the passion seem unreal.

Dorian Gray turned pale while he watched. He felt confused and worried. Neither of his friends dared speak to him. To them she appeared completely unable to act.

At noon on Saturday I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning powders that gave off smoke, clawing at the air, and muttering nonsense as vigorously as ever. He looked rather discouraged, though, since he had not managed to make the well produce so much as a drop of sweat. Finally I said:

“How are our prospects looking now, partner?”

“As you see, I am testing the most powerful enchantment known to the masters of the occult in the East. If this fails, nothing can help. Be silent until I finish.”

This time he produced enough smoke to darken the whole area. It must have been unpleasant for the hermits, because the wind carried it towards them and it billowed down over their shelters in a thick fog. His flood of words matched the smoke. He twisted himself into extraordinary shapes and chopped at the air with both hands. After twenty minutes he collapsed, panting and nearly worn out. The abbot now arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, followed by a mass of pilgrims and a couple of acres of abandoned children. The prodigious smoke had attracted them all, and everyone was wildly excited. The abbot anxiously asked what had been achieved. Merlin answered:

“If any human effort could break the spell that holds these waters captive, the enchantment I just attempted would have done it. It has failed. I now know that what I feared is true: the mightiest spirit known to the Eastern magicians, whose name no one may speak and survive, has enchanted this well. No mortal alive, or yet to be born, can discover that spell’s secret. Without the secret, no one can undo it. These waters will never flow again, good Father. I have done everything a man can do. Allow me to leave.”

Naturally, this upset the abbot considerably. He turned to me, his alarm plain on his face, and asked:

“You heard him. Is it true?”

“Some of it.”

“Then not everything! Which part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast a spell over the well.”

“By God’s wounds, we’re ruined!”

“Perhaps.”

“But we aren’t certain to be? Is that what you mean?”

“Exactly.”

“So you also mean that when he says nobody can break the spell—”

“Yes. That part isn’t necessarily true. Under certain conditions, an attempt to break it might have a chance—a small chance, a very slight one—of succeeding.”

‘Oh, never mind my hat! I want Virginia!’ the little Duke cried, laughing, and they galloped onward to the railway station. Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anybody resembling Virginia had been noticed on the platform, but learned nothing of her whereabouts. The station-master nevertheless telegraphed in both directions along the line and promised that a careful lookout would be maintained. After purchasing a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper just closing his shutters, Mr. Otis set out for Bexley, a village some four miles distant. He had been informed that gypsies frequented the place because of the extensive common adjoining it. They woke the country policeman there, but he had no information to give. Having ridden across the entire common, they turned their mounts towards home, arriving at the Chase around eleven, utterly exhausted and nearly broken-hearted. Washington and the twins awaited them with lanterns at the gate-house, for the avenue lay in deep darkness. No hint of Virginia’s presence had been found. The gypsies had been overtaken in Brockley meadows, but she was not among them. They explained their abrupt departure by saying they had confused the date of Chorton Fair and hurried away for fear of arriving too late. Indeed, the news of Virginia’s disappearance distressed them greatly. They felt much gratitude to Mr. Otis for permitting them to camp in his park, and four of them had remained to assist the search. The carp pond had been dragged and every part of the Chase carefully examined, all to no purpose. Clearly, for that night at least, Virginia remained lost to them. In profound dejection Mr. Otis and the boys walked towards the house, followed by the groom leading the two horses and the pony. A frightened knot of servants stood in the hall. In the library poor Mrs. Otis lay upon a sofa, almost beside herself with fear and anxiety, while the elderly housekeeper bathed her brow with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and directed that supper be brought for everyone. It was a sorrowful meal. Scarcely a word was spoken, and even the twins, who loved their sister dearly, were hushed and frightened. Once they had finished, Mr. Otis sent them all to bed despite the little Duke’s pleading. Nothing further could be accomplished that night, he said; in the morning he would wire Scotland Yard and request that detectives be dispatched without delay.
